storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of thunderstorm cells is essentially on top of the cove right now, and with no protective Sound effect in play tonight, expect wind, rain, and lightning within minutes rather than a weakened pass-through.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (74°F) and air (72°F) are nearly the same temperature tonight, so there's no stabilizing marine layer to blunt this storm the way there sometimes is on hotter, muggier days.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows an active cluster of thunderstorm cells sitting almost directly over Riverside and Greenwich Cove, with several cells producing 45–52 dBZ reflectivity within a few miles of the coastline and the nearest cell just under a mile away at scan time. CAPE is a moderate 910 J/kg with 0–6 km shear around 16 kt right now — enough to organize convection but not an extreme severe-weather setup. No NWS watches or warnings are posted for the area at this time, but the radar picture is unambiguous: this is happening at the cove, not somewhere else on the map.

The usual Riverside “protective bubble” is not available tonight. The Sound is running about 74.5°F against 71.6°F air — only a -2.9°F delta — so there is no meaningful stable marine layer sitting over the water to choke incoming convection. Sound-effect likelihood is negligible and the protective mechanism is inactive. Expect this storm to hit Riverside essentially as advertised, with the same intensity surrounding towns are seeing.

The cove-specific arrival engine, anchored to a fresh radar scan and using measured (not modeled) storm motion, has the nearest cell 3 mi NNW of the cove closing at 17 kt with a 9-minute ETA — arrival around 6:04–6:05 PM. This is not an isolated pulse: four more cells in the same cluster are queued in behind it with ETAs spread from 6:03 to 6:09 PM, so expect a rolling passage of wind, rain, and lightning over the cove for a while rather than one quick hit.

What would change the call: instability is trending up, not down, through the window — HRRR shows shear building from 16 kt now to 24–26 kt and CAPE rising toward roughly 1400 J/kg by 9–10 PM. That raises the odds of renewed or strengthening storms later in the evening rather than a clean clearance after this first cluster passes. Worth rechecking radar as the evening goes on rather than assuming one pass-through is the whole story.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 3 mi NNW closing at 17 kt; with no marine layer in play tonight, expect it close to on schedule rather than late or weakened.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light, wandering gradient flow (3–4 kt) is being overrun by a cluster of thunderstorm cells passing directly over the cove through the evening — expect sudden gusty shifts during each cell's passage rather than any steady favored side. Stay off the water until the storms clear, then expect a return to light, shifty gradient breeze.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a light gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day: the air–water temperature difference is only -2.9°F, well short of the 5°F needed to build a thermal, and the sea-breeze flag is off. With the thermal driver absent, this falls to gradient-only classification, and the background flow itself is light — the authoritative station average is just 3.9 kt, putting it in the light-gradient bucket where direction tends to wander rather than hold a clean axis.

Normally a light-gradient evening like this would call for racing the middle of the course and picking off small local puffs. Tonight that call is overridden by an active thunderstorm cluster sitting essentially on top of the cove (see the storm section) — the wind field right now is fragmented rather than coherent: direction agreement across the station network is only 26%, far below the ~70% that would indicate a settled flow. That kind of scatter is consistent with multiple gust fronts and outflow boundaries moving through rather than one clean gradient direction, and it means any “favored side” call is unreliable until the cells clear.

Because this is a gradient-only (Regime B) evening rather than a sea-breeze day, the HRRR sea-breeze direction-maturation correction does not apply — there is no thermal veer to correct for, so the raw HRRR directions (SW backing to SSW, then WSW) are used as-is for the forecast hours, though confidence in them is low while convection is active.

What racers would actually feel: RYC itself is reading almost dead calm (0.4 kt, gust 2.8 kt, SSE) in the lull just ahead of the lead cell, which is the calm-before-the-gust-front pattern typical of an approaching thunderstorm. Once each cell's outflow crosses, expect a short, sharp spike in wind speed and a hard direction swing, followed by a drop back to light and variable. This is not a night to sail through — sit it out until the cluster clears, then expect an unremarkable 3–4 kt shifty gradient breeze for the remainder of the window, with a chance of renewed activity late as shear and CAPE both trend upward into the 9–10 PM hours.
